author: Han Kang
introFa: کتاب «The White Book» نوشته Han Kang یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The White Book»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

In his entirely original ﬁfth book, which is just about exactly as long as the ﬁrst four combined, he presents a history of the entire Dominican reform in Teutonia, focusing on both male and female houses. Jones prefaces all this with a succinct but valuable introduction. In just thirty pages, she lays out what one needs to know about the Dominican order, its reform, Johannes Meyer, and the technical aspects of his work. An old edition exists, published in 1908. She, however, translates from a different manuscript, now in Strasbourg, which, she argues, is likely closest to Meyer’s original. That manuscript will be the basis for a planned critical edition by Christian Seebald of the University of Siegen, with which Jones intends her translation to be compatible. Because of both the previous and planned editions, she keeps her critical apparatus constrained, but she provides helpful notes throughout the text, making her trans- lation navigable even for undergraduates (clearly an intended audience, as the paperback edi- tion is priced for classroom use). Jones stresses Meyer’s acumen as a historian. He looked at documents and spoke to wit- nesses whenever he could, and he synthesized to present his own analysis. There remains a lot of “chronicle” about this work, of course: the life of this sister after the life of that sister, the reform of this house after the reform of that one. This comes, however, with a wealth of detail about innumerable aspects of the late medieval religious world. The overriding theme is standard for the Observants: corruption and decline, and the intransigent opposition that reformers confronted at every turn. As Jones highlights, reform was a complex process invol- ving not just the order itself but also bishops and other clergy, sometimes even popes, as well as secular ofﬁcials from the localities in which reformed houses lay. As she also notes, when other accounts of reform survive, they often present a far less contentious picture than the reformers painted for themselves. Nevertheless, Meyer gives us a clear notion of reformers’ self-conception, if not always of their reality. Jones’s valuable translation offers students and experts alike access to this very important source. Michael D. Bailey, Iowa State University Michael Jones, Julia Barrow, David Crook, and Trevor Foulds, eds., The White Book (“Liber Albus”) of Southwell, with contributions from Neil Bettridge, Jean Cameron, Paul Cavill, and Teresa Webber, 2 vols. (Publications of the Pipe Roll Society 61.) Woodbridge, UK: Boydell for the Pipe Roll Society, 2018. Pp. cxiv, 805; 2 color plates, 10 black-and-white ﬁgures, and 3 maps. $170. ISBN: 978-0-9011-3467-7. Table of contents available online at https://boydellandbrewer.com/the-white-book-i-liber -albus-i-of-southwell.html doi:10.1086/710674 As the register of its county’s most prominent secular church, The White Book of Southwell is an important source for the history of medieval Nottinghamshire. Southwell Minster and its sister churches at Beverley and Ripon served as supplementary cathedrals to the archbishop of York. As the archbishop held the advowson of its prebends, he appointed some of his house- hold clergy to them, sometimes in addition to their holding prebends or archdeaconries at York Minster or elsewhere; but also like other secular collegiate churches of cathedral and noncathedral status, its chapter included both royal and papal bureaucrats as well as sons of prominent local families. Its records thus shed light not only on the clerical activities that took place within its sanctuary and famous chapter house, but also on the careers of men who played a larger part in the business of church and state. Like most great churches, its religious functions were possible only because it held landed estates and appropriated parishes. The documents demonstrating their rights over and man- agement of these provide much of the material the canons recorded in the White Book. Not Reviews 1185 Speculum 95/4 (October 2020)

everything the chapter chose to immortalize in its pages seems of equal weight, however. Among its important statutes, charters, and papal letters can be found documents of more transitory signiﬁcance, such as an inquest into the value of a deceased canon’s estate (no. 200). In this way it is as much a register as it is a cartulary. This variety of content makes it a rich and interesting source. While the edition is so thor- ough that it is hard to imagine its ever being superseded, it opens rather than closes doors. (Where a document has been printed elsewhere, the text is still provided here in full.) The sto- ries touched on in the documents and editors’ notes could suggest to thoughtful readers the cores of many potential articles and will furnish readily available examples to historians working on topics ranging from local history and vicars choral to manumissions from serf- dom and the Assize of Bread and Ale. Legal history is represented in sections on the liberties and manor courts (nos. 142–84), recording the exercise of the chapter’s secular authority in a selection of cases that they evidently thought worth preserving for posterity. The editors and contributors provide extensive commentary. The introduction, covering the contents, the manuscript, and the composition of the chapter, is over eighty pages long. Volume 2 concludes with more than one hundred pages of appendices. The introduction includes an analysis of changing norms of diplomatic practice; this could be used, together with the cited examples in the documents, as a teaching text. The plates showing paleographical samples may be too small for some readers to make out, though descriptions of some hands are quite vivid, as for instance the “unidentiﬁed rather scrappy late medieval Anglicana hand under Secretary inﬂuence” that wrote no. 587. Documents are preceded by an English sum- mary and followed by notes addressing not only the text, date, and manuscript features but also the individuals and locations in the document and how they related to the Minster and to one another. Some notes are quite extensive: no. 77, a document only nine lines long, is followed by almost two pages of notes. Many of the documents in the “Pleas in the Manor Courts” section relate to a single property that was in dispute when its holder died without heirs at the time of the Black Death (see especially no. 171n). The White Book traces that property and its holders over many generations, from before 1250 to the ﬁfteenth century, but it would have been difﬁcult to make sense of it were it not for the notes. The editors are clear that while their edition of theWhite Book furnishes material for a prosopo- graphical study, actually providing such a study is beyond their ambitions here (lxxxi). The appendices include a “Summary Fasti of Canons and Prebends of Southwell.” The names are presented only in alphabetical order without any attempt to reconstruct the succession to particular prebends (which is often not possible in any case) or to list individuals chrono- logically (which at least would have helped to identify contemporaries). Yet it provides a full list of canons the editors found in their research, not just those mentioned in the documents. A separate citation follows each datum, which is far preferable to piling all the citations at the end of an entry, as some other editors have done. In his preface, Michael Jones describes how the edition grew unexpectedly from a much more modest exercise in local history. But there is nothing modest about the labor the editors and con- tributors expended to complete these volumes for the Pipe Roll Society. Like Southwell Minster itself, this edition is a monument of singular charms that should ably stand the test of time. William H. Campbell, University of Pittsburgh, Greensburg 1186 Reviews Speculum 95/4 (October 2020)
